blocks.text: We must now say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we said, other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in the Geography of Nubia, Clim. 1, section 1, interprets it as white weasel. Golius renders it mustela foenaria [hay weasel], commonly fovina [beech marten] (for that most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alludes to foenum [hay], and that fovina is named from foenum, whereas it takes its name from the French word for the beech). For Giggeius فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain very useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are taken. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farʾāʾ yujlab kathīran] [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmihi ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalī ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn libs al-fanak] The phenec is an animal whose skin is warm and of good odour, the most fragrant among all kinds of furs. It is brought in great quantity from Secalia. Its flesh seems to be sweet. Its skin is colder than the skin of the simor, but warmer than the skin of the sungiab. It is the custom above all to be clothed in this skin in advancing age. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-al-qamāqim wa-al-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa] The skins alphenec, and alkamakim, and alhawasil are of moderate warmth, and light besides. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwaybba yūkhadh minhā al-farw qāl Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-farāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb] Alphenec, a small animal from which fur is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and is brought in great quantity from the Sclavic region: so it should be read above, not صقالية [Ṣaqāliya] Secalia (the Sclavic region, that is, of the Sclavs, was formerly in European Scythia towards the western Ocean, as Simocatta testifies, book 6, chapter 2). Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghahyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-al-sinjāb wa-al-sammūr kull dhālika sabʿ ka-al-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs] The phenec, the sungiab and the simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. So they say; from which it might seem to follow that these skins belong to species of marten. Yet الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec po[?]

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls Venetian and Agricola Finnic, from the Veneti and the Finns, peoples on the Vistula in Prussia, from whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy says in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι· [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi] By the river Vistula, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finns. From these Finns, I say, the Finnic mouse seems to be named, and in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec, which from its size and colour the French call petit-gris ^{(4)}. But سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab too is for Golius the squirrel, an animal of ash-grey colour, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says it is an animal shaped like a mole, larger than a mouse, living in the tops of trees, with a bluish skin, very soft and very beautiful, in which the refined are clothed. It is evident that a species of squirrel is described. The simur too is a kind of mouse, not wholly unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais] [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας· [chrōntai pros chitōnas] Among the Parthians a certain species of wild mouse is called simor, whose skins are used for garments. For others the simur is the marten. Damir says it is an animal like the cat, or, in the opinion of some, like the ferret, النمس [al-nims], whose skin so excels in softness, lightness, warmth and beauty that kings and nobles are clothed in it. I could add much more about both skins, drawn from the books of the Arabs; but explaining these details more precisely is not for our leisure, nor does it much concern the present matter.
Among the Greeks there is equal inconsistency in explaining the word שפן saphan.
1. There are some who render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous] [hares], like the Vulgate translator, little hares: which we have already examined above.

2. There were some who preferred the hyena, like Clement of Alexandria, Paedagogus, book 2, chapter 10, where he introduces Moses saying: Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is, הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what is read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], But neither shall you eat the hare. And a little later, Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has Sed nec belluam manducabis [But neither shall you eat the beast]. I would prefer beluum or belbum. For so Julius Capitolinus in the third Gordian: There were at Rome under Gordian 32 elephants, 10 elks, 10 tigers, 60 tame lions, 30 tame leopards [II, 418] 10 belbi, that is, hyenas. Yet in the Glossary of Philoxenus: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina· zōon], bellua [beast].
